\section{The Class-Level Calculation, in Full}
\label{app:classes}
% ===========================================================================

Every quantity that determines the class split, including the declared
energy intensities that weight it. The within-fuel weights are the
$s_{c,f}$ of the main paper's methods section: vehicle-kilometres times
MJ/km, normalised within each fuel over \emph{all} classes including
off-road, which is the deliberate normalisation that lets the two
categories partition one diesel quantity. Because the weights sum to one
by construction, the intensities move composition and never magnitude.
Machine-readable: \texttt{outputs/transport\_class\_parameters\_2024.csv}.

On distance alone it would be 0.8119, and the difference between those two numbers is the whole correction -- a motorcycle-kilometre and a car-kilometre are not the same quantity of petrol. The intensities are declared engineering judgement, not Pakistani measurement, which is why they are confined to a normalisation that cannot move the sector total.}
\label{tab:classweights}

The off-road partition share, with its actual inputs -- energy, not
distance, because the same normalisation that splits the on-road classes
sets this share:
\begin{equation*}
s_{\text{offroad}} = \frac{1.252e+10}{1.252e+10 + 1.286e+11} = 0.08871,
\end{equation*}
in megajoules of declared fleet energy, which carves \SI{21177}{\tera\joule} from the Road-row diesel control. The numerator is the off-road class's 941,248 active vehicles at \SI{1900}{\kilo\metre} each at \SI{7}{\mega\joule\per\kilo\metre}; on distance alone the share was 0.09998, and it falls because off-road machinery burns LESS per kilometre than the on-road diesel fleet average (7 MJ/km against roughly 9.5, a mean dominated by buses and heavy goods vehicles) -- weighting by energy shrinks the off-road share and moves diesel back to the road category. The \texttt{offroad\_share\_5pct} and \texttt{15pct} scenarios price the share's softness.
